newsitem.title: USA: USDA coffee production data seen bearish - analysts.
newsitem.headline: USDA coffee production data seen bearish - analysts.

text.p: U.S. analysts and traders said world coffee production estimates put out by the U.S. Department of Agriculture on Friday were bearish and likely to weigh on the futures market.

In its bi-annual World Agricultural Production report, the USDA estimated world coffee production in 1997/98 would rise to 103.7 million bags, from 100.7 million bags the previous season. World output in 1997/98 would match the previous record harvest produced in the 1991/92 season, it said.

"That is negative," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "At 103.7 million, you're looking at a stock build. Those people who were looking for $4 (per lb) are probably going to be looking at $1.50 soon."

USDA forecast the 1997/98 crop from top-grower Brazil would come in at 28 million bags, compared with a revised 27.5 million bags in 1996/97. The USDA's 1996/97 forecast is slightly higher than a 27 million bag estimate issued in December.
Early estimates from the trade in Brazil have put next season's crop at anywhere from 18 to 25 million 60-kg bags, versus an estimated 1996/97 yield of at least 25 million.
"It throws a lot of cold water on those preliminary Brazil estimates looking at 20 million," Platt commented.
But most U.S.-based traders said they expected the USDA figure for 1997/98 to surpass the Brazil trade forecasts.
"It's bearish," said one trader. "But I think the report is particially factored into the market. The market sold-off on expectations it would be around 28 million."
U.S. traders were baffled, however, by the USDA's modest revision of Brazil's 1996/97 coffee crop, which puts it below the coming 1997/98 harvest.
"The Brazilians have shipped so much in the first half of this year, most people think the crop is around 30 million bags," said another trader.

Traders said the USDA's forecasts for second-largest producer Colombia were mostly in line with expectations. USDA pegged the 1997/98 crop at 11.3 million bags, versus a downwardly revised 1996/97 crop of 10.3 million bags.

Although the revision for the 1996/97 crop was substantial -- the USDA pegged Colombia's 1996/97 harvest at 12.5 million bags in December -- traders said talk of reduced Colombia production has been priced in the market and contributed to coffee's stunning rally since the end of last year.
But since July coffee futures rocketed to 20-year high of 318.00 cents per lb two weeks ago, values have tumbled by some 38 percent and traders said sentiment has turned negative.
"The USDA numbers are just a confirmation of the downtrend," said one trader. "Three weeks ago it would have been a lot more bearish."

Traders and analysts warned, however, the market's bearish tone could quickly turn bullish at any sign of chilly weather in Brazil. Brazil is entering the most risky period for damaging cold, they noted. Two severe frosts in 1994, one in June and another in July, wiped out coffee trees and sent futures prices rocketing.
Market participants now await the Green Coffee Association of New York's May inventory data due Monday at 1500 EDT/1900 GMT.

Most industry participants expected aggressive shipments by producers to build stockpiles in the U.S. by some 150,000-250,000 bags in May, although estimates for an increase ranged broadly from 25,000 to 400,000 bagsr.

Last month, the GCA reported U.S. consumer coffee stocks rose by 198,000 bags in April, to 1,855,000 bags. In May 1996, however, coffee stowed in U.S. warehouses stood at 2,271,000 bags, down 25,000 from the previous month.
-- Patricia Avidan, New York Commodity Desk, +1 212 859 1640
